stories.title: Kenya: Six Oil Tankers Among 51 Ships Expected At Mombasa, Lamu Ports
stories.summary: Kenya: Six Oil Tankers Among 51 Ships Expected At Mombasa, Lamu Ports 21 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Bruhan Makong Mombasa — Kenya's two seaports are expected to handle 51 vessels over the next 14 days, including six oil tankers scheduled to dock at the Port of Mombasa. The Kenya Ports Authority (KPA) said Mombasa would receive 41 vessels, comprising six oil tankers, 26 container ships, seven conventional cargo vessels and two car carriers. The Port of Lamu is projected to handle 10 vessels over the same period, including nine container ships and one general cargo vessel. The latest projection represents an increase from the 45 vessels KPA forecast on October 7, when Mombasa was expected to receive 34 ships and Lamu 11. The new outlook points to a higher number of vessel calls across the two ports, with Mombasa accounting for the bulk of the anticipated maritime traffic.

stories.title: Kenya: Government Elevates Illicit Alcohol Trade to Organised Crime
stories.summary: Kenya: Government Elevates Illicit Alcohol Trade to Organised Crime 21 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) Nairobi — Deputy President Kithure Kindiki says the government has elevated the manufacture, distribution, sale and consumption of illicit alcohol to the category of organised crime, placing it alongside terrorism and banditry in its enforcement framework. Kindiki said the government would take firm action against cartels involved in the illicit alcohol trade, accusing them of threatening the lives of young people and the country's future. "Government has also elevated the manufacturing, distribution, sale and consumption of illicit alcohol as organised crime, listing it in the category of terrorism and banditry, and directed firm action against cartels destroying the youth and by extension, the country's future," read a communique after the meeting. Speaking after chairing a follow-up review meeting on the fight against illicit alcohol and drugs at his Karen Residence in Nairobi, the Deputy President said security agencies would be allowed to conduct intelligence-led operations without political interference. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He warned that the government would not tolerate the politicisation of the campaign, insisting that enforcement agencies must be given room to conduct raids, make arrests and pursue prosecutions. Kindiki said the government had established a permanent multi-agency secretariat in the Office of the Deputy President to coordinate the crackdown and ensure operations are sustained. "The secretariat will be at the 6th Floor, Harambee House, and will include representatives from the National Police Service, Kenya Bureau of Standards, NACADA, Anti Counterfeit Authority, Alcohol manufacturers association, NIS, DCI, EACC, Ministry of Trade, Ministry of Health, KRA," Kindiki stated.

The introductory meeting focused on strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation between Somalia and the European Union, with a particular emphasis on EU support for infrastructure development and state institutions. Ambassador Máthé reaffirmed the EU's commitment to continuing its support for development projects across both the Federal Member States and the Federal Government of Somalia to bolster national progress. stories.summary: Tanzania: BoT Records Rise in Monetary Gold Holdings 21 October 2026 Tanzania Daily News (Dar es Salaam) Dar es Salaam — THE Bank of Tanzania's gold holdings rose by 3.6 per cent in September, strengthening the gold component of its assets and highlighting the importance of precious metals in the central bank's financial position. The Bank's Statement of Financial Position as at September this year shows that the combined monetary gold and gold bullion holdings increased to 10.60tri/- from 10.24tri/- in August, a rise of approximately 365.3bn/-. Monetary gold increased to 3.43tri/- from 3.16tri/-, while gold bullion rose to 7.17tri/- from 7.08tri/-, contributing to the overall growth in the two categories. The increase highlights the changing composition of the central bank's assets, with gold holdings accounting for a substantial share of its total assets. However, the monthly figures do not establish whether the rise resulted from additional purchases, valuation changes or other transactions.

stories.title: Liberia: Konneh Says Country's Growth Is Bypassing Citizens
stories.summary: Liberia: Konneh Says Country's Growth Is Bypassing Citizens 21 October 2026 Liberian Observer (Monrovia) Gbarpolu County Senator Amara M. Konneh has warned that Liberia's improving economic growth figures are failing to translate into meaningful improvements in citizens' living conditions, pointing to rising living costs, weak implementation of public investment projects, limited agricultural growth and gaps in petroleum-levy collections. Reporting to the Liberian Senate on Tuesday following his constituency break, Konneh used his address to connect the challenges facing rural communities with broader concerns about public financial management, the national budget and the government's development priorities. His central argument was that economic growth must be judged not only by gross domestic product (GDP), revenue collection or the size of the national budget, but also by whether citizens have access to roads, functioning schools, healthcare, security and employment opportunities. "The government is right, and the numbers it has announced are true," Konneh said of the reported economic expansion. "But the people are right, too. They are not feeling it." stories.summary: Africa Needs More Than Envoys to Secure the Red Sea 21 October 2026 Institute for Security Studies (Tshwane/Pretoria) analysis By Moses Chrispus Okello The Horn's proliferating diplomatic appointments have done little to bolster African influence amid new Middle Eastern alliances. In September, Ansarullah (the Houthis) took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, shattering the assumption that the insurgency was confined to northern Yemen. The group is now at the epicentre of the Middle East conflict and is the channel through which crises flow between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East. Countries on either side of the Red Sea have responded asymmetrically to this shared shock. The Horn has dispatched more envoys while Middle Eastern countries, led by Saudi Arabia, are strengthening political institutions and hardwiring them with military deals.

RFI spoke to Libya specialist Virginie Collombier about what "Khadafism" stood for, who still believes in it and whether the removal of its architect has made life better for the country's people. Kadhafi seized power in Libya in a military coup in 1969 and went on to build one of the most idiosyncratic states of the 20th century. Funded by vast oil wealth and enforced by ruthless repression, it was guided by his Green Book - a manifesto proposing a "third way" between capitalism and communism, and officially called the Jamahiriya - or "state of the masses". Kadhafi cast himself as a champion of Arab - and subsequently African - liberation, and backed armed groups abroad, which brought years of Western and United Nations sanctions.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said. A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF. The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.

Another 15 countries have expressed intent to join the initiative, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) is targeting all 55 African Union Member States to participate in the APPM. The announcement came at the conclusion of the third APPM Member States Consultative Workshop held in Addis Ababa, marking a shift from political commitment to implementation, in line with African Union directives. Established by an African Union Assembly decision in February 2024, the APPM is spearheaded by Africa CDC to strengthen collective purchasing of essential health products across the continent. By pooling demand from Member States, the APPM aims to improve access to affordable, quality-assured health products, strengthen supply security, reduce procurement costs and create predictable, sustainable markets for African manufacturers.

Photograph: Monicah Mwangi/Reuters Explainer Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat Country has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returns Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion. Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war. The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993.

Illustration: Chronicle/Alamy Obituary Tim Jeal obituary Biographer who altered perceptions of Henry Morton Stanley, David Livingstone, Robert Baden-Powell and other figures active in Africa Thanks to the biographer and novelist Tim Jeal, who has died aged 81, we now know that one of the most famous sentences in journalism – “Dr Livingstone, I presume?” – was almost certainly never uttered. In November 1871, after a 700-mile expedition, the Welsh-American journalist and adventurer Henry Morton Stanley tracked down David Livingstone, the Scottish missionary and explorer. He had been lost to the outside world for six years and was now nearing death, in Ujiji, on the shores of Lake Tanganyika in present-day Tanzania.

Photograph: AP LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report . More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.” Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

stories.title: Ghana's Semenyo 'froze' after alleged racist abuse, court told
stories.summary: Image source, Press Association Image caption, Antoine Semenyo was playing for Bournemouth when the alleged incident happened during a match against Liverpool in August 2025 Published 14 October 2026 Footballer Antoine Semenyo "froze" after he was allegedly racially abused by a Liverpool fan during a Premier League match at Anfield, a court has heard. The Manchester City winger, who was playing for Bournemouth at the time, was preparing to take a throw-in when Mark Mogan, 47, allegedly shouted a racist insult at him on 15 August 2025. Prosecutors said Semenyo was "clearly hurt and upset" and reported the incident to referee Anthony Taylor when the ball next went out of play. Mogan, of Dovecot, Liverpool, denies racially aggravated behaviour. Liverpool Magistrates' Court heard Mogan, who uses a wheelchair, shouted an offensive slur about 30 minutes into the opening match of the Premier League season.
